content:
Disability Living Allowance (DLA) is now mainly for children under 16 in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, including children with juvenile arthritis. Most adults cannot make a new claim for DLA. Adults of working age claim Personal Independence Payment (PIP), or Adult Disability Payment in Scotland. People over State Pension age claim Attendance Allowance, or Pension Age Disability Payment in Scotland.

DLA for children with arthritis

Children with arthritis, such as juvenile idiopathic arthritis, may qualify for DLA if they need much more care or supervision than other children of the same age, or have difficulty walking. There are two parts:

  • care component, paid at one of three rates, for help with personal care, supervision or attention day and night
  • mobility component, paid at one of two rates, for difficulty walking or needing supervision outdoors

The child must usually have needed this help for at least three months and be expected to need it for at least six more. Claims are made by a parent or carer.

In Scotland, DLA for children has been replaced by Child Disability Payment, run by Social Security Scotland.

Tips for a child's claim

  • describe a typical day and a bad day, including mornings, school, nights and flares
  • explain help needed with dressing, washing, toileting, eating, getting about, taking medicines and attending appointments
  • include supervision needs, such as managing pain or medicine side effects
  • add evidence from the rheumatology team, school, physiotherapist or occupational therapist
  • keep a diary for a week or two before filling in the form

What happens at 16

When a child on DLA turns 16, they are usually invited to apply for PIP. In Scotland, Child Disability Payment can continue until 18 and then moves to Adult Disability Payment.

Adults already on DLA

Most adults who were on DLA have been moved to PIP. If you were born on or before 8 April 1948, you may still receive DLA as long as you remain eligible. Report any changes in your condition.

PIP for working-age adults

PIP helps with the extra costs of a long-term health condition or disability. It is not means-tested and you can claim whether you work or not. It is based on how your arthritis affects you, not the diagnosis. There are two parts:

  • daily living, for difficulties with tasks such as preparing food, washing, dressing and managing medicines
  • mobility, for difficulties planning journeys or moving around

For arthritis, think about pain, stiffness, fatigue and flares, and whether you can do tasks safely, to an acceptable standard, repeatedly and in a reasonable time.

Adult Disability Payment in Scotland

Adult Disability Payment replaced PIP for people living in Scotland. It has a similar structure but is run by Social Security Scotland, which aims to avoid unnecessary face-to-face assessments.

Attendance Allowance for older people

If you are over State Pension age and need help with personal care or supervision because of arthritis, you may be able to claim Attendance Allowance. There is no mobility part. It is not means-tested. In Scotland, Pension Age Disability Payment is replacing it.

Other help to check

  • Carer's Allowance for someone who cares for you for at least 35 hours a week
  • Blue Badge for parking if walking is very difficult
  • Motability, if you receive the higher mobility rate
  • council tax reduction and help with health costs
  • Universal Credit if you are on a low income or cannot work

Getting help with a claim

Free advice is available from Citizens Advice and local welfare rights services. Some hospitals have benefits advisers. If you disagree with a decision, you can ask for a mandatory reconsideration, and then appeal to a tribunal. Many decisions are changed at appeal, so it is worth challenging a decision you think is wrong.

Keeping up to date

Benefit rules and rates change, often each April. Always check the latest details on GOV.UK or mygov.scot before you apply.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.
